content: I've been implementing sound and complete Hilbert systems for propositional logic including the minimal, intuitionistic, and classical systems, establishing soundness and completeness for each. I also established the extensional equivalence with the intuitionistic and classical natural deduction systems. Still working on clean up, but here is what I have so far: https://github.com/benbrastmckie/cslib/tree/main/Cslib/Logics/Propositional
So I want to build on this PR, although all I need is assignment expression semantics at the moment. Would it be possible to make a smaller PR with just these semantics and maybe strong soundness?

Hi Matthew, sorry I never got back to you in the other thread it completely slipped my mind! I think the right generality to develop assignment expressions + soundness (which i am interpreting as a Bool or Prop valued interpretation of a PL proposition) is in a docs#GeneralizedHeytingAlgebra — the proof is practically the same & this way it captures minimal and intuitionistic logic too. There are a couple of open PRs on ND already so I've held off PRing my work on the topic, but if you wanted to pick this up as a topic to work on i'd be very happy to see it moving!

& hi also Benjamin :) I think your Hilbert-style approach is certainly interesting, as it happens i had been sketching something very similar in a branch which i find promising. i had an equivalent of your "derivation system" under the name "contextual inference system" with a similar interest in systems validating eg the deduction theorem, and also (in the same file) a simple hilbert-style derivation system.
i do think however that the design of something this general would require a fair amount of discussion, which makes PRing small pieces at a time important. that being said, i'd be excited to review steps in this direction!

also Matthew, picking up on the points in the other thread — i think the idea of machinery to automate appeals to propositional logic is very interesting. the proof i had is constructive, and modulo the decidability of something being a classical tautology could construct an ND proof of propositions. i think the right way to do this for more general logics would be a class, though, like you said. i'd be very interested to see how this would work :) i unfortunately don't know anything about probability logic, though the folks at formalised formal logic might have more to say.

Hi Thomas and Matthey! I'm excited to contribute to contribute to this. I've been working backwards from the Bimodal logic that I established completeness for (which was all classical), so have been refactoring the propositional foundations to align with the ND system in CSLib.

I established the deduction theorem and strong soundness and completeness for the minimal/inuitionistic/classical Hilbert systems and then proved their equivalence to the ND systems so that the ND systems inherit these results. This is typical since Hilbert systems are a lot easier to work with for establishing metalogical results. I've been trying to clean everything up and carve it up into small pieces for PRs. I would be curious to know what you think. Here are some links:

- deductionTheorem
- min_strong_completeness
- int_strong_completeness
- prop_strong_completeness

One issue regarding the syntax is that bot is not currently taken to be a primitive constructor in Proposition/, but rather simulated via [Bot Atom]. I created a PR to fix this, providing a foundation that will support the Hilbert systems for the Propositional/, Temporal/, and Bimodal/ logics and would be curious to get any thoughts.

Well, I had been thinking of proving Strong Soundness/Completeness, but @Benjamin Brast-McKie beat me to it, so I thought I'd pivot to porting John Harrison's Handbook of Practical Logic and Automated Reasoning.

So far I've just given interpretation semantics for Atom -> Bool models for propositional formulae and CNF expressions, and proved that the Tseitin transformation from Proposition Atom to CNF is equisatisfiable.

The short-term goal would be to prove DPLL works as a decision procedure for propositional logic, if that makes sense. But we could also try to port and verify MiniSAT if there's interest.

I see that @Benjamin Brast-McKie 's models are from Atom -> Prop; would it be possible to switch to Atom -> Bool? In my case, I'd argue Atom -> Bool will be more portable for implementing DPLL for finding models.

also Matthew, picking up on the points in the other thread — i think the idea of machinery to automate appeals to propositional logic is very interesting. the proof i had is constructive, and modulo the decidability of something being a classical tautology could construct an ND proof of propositions. i think the right way to do this for more general logics would be a class, though, like you said. i'd be very interested to see how this would work :) i unfortunately don't know anything about probability logic, though the folks at formalised formal logic might have more to say.

If you look at the Wikipedia page for probability logic, it's a bit of a mess, but a landmark result is Fagin et al.'s A Logic for Reasoning about Probabilities, where they give a complete axiomatization of Boolean combinations of inequalities in probability theory, and show that their theory is decidable and NP-Complete. If this seems appropriate, it might be nice to tackle formalizing this result in Lean...

Another idea is to define a finitely additive probability function Pr : Proposition Atom -> [0,1] and take some classical logic ⊢ and give the axioms Pr(ϕ) ≥ 0, ⊢ ϕ ⟹ Pr(ϕ) = 1, and Pr(ϕ) + Pr(ψ) = Pr(ϕ ∧ ψ) + Pr(ϕ ∨ ψ) (or something equivalent for the last axiom). A rather old result by Patrick Suppes I'm fond of in this setting is Γ ⊢ ϕ ⇔ ∀ Pr. ∑{1 − Pr(γ) | γ ∈ Γ} ≥ 1 − Pr(ϕ) for finite Γ. You can prove this using the MCS machinery that @Benjamin Brast-McKie is developing.

Matthew Doty said:

I see that @Benjamin Brast-McKie 's models are from Atom -> Prop; would it be possible to switch to Atom -> Bool? In my case, I'd argue Atom -> Bool will be more portable for implementing DPLL for finding models.

Hi Matthew, that's a great question. The core Valuation type needs to stay Atom → Prop because the canonical model construction in strong completeness uses fun p => atom p ∈ S where S is an MCS built via Lindenbaum/Zorn — that set membership is inherently Prop-valued with no DecidablePred. The same → Prop convention runs through the modal, temporal, and bimodal Kripke semantics.

To get Bool for DPLL, I think the answer is to have both: I've added a BoolEvaluate : (Atom → Bool) → Proposition Atom → Bool alongside the existing Evaluate, with a bridge lemma BoolEvaluate v φ = true ↔ Evaluate (fun a => v a = true) φ. That's a small addition that gives you computable evaluation connected to the existing metatheory including prop_strong_soundness.

Both layers are provided in the commit I just pushed to PR 648: Semantics/Basic.lean defines the Prop-valued Evaluate and Tautology, and Semantics/Bool.lean adds BoolEvaluate with the bridge lemma and a Decidable instance. Happy to adjust if you think there is a better way to structure it for DPLL module, or feel free to stack a PR. Let me know!

Benjamin Brast-McKie said:

Hi Matthew, that's a great question. The core Valuation type needs to stay Atom → Prop because the canonical model construction in strong completeness uses fun p => atom p ∈ S where S is an MCS built via Lindenbaum/Zorn — that set membership is inherently Prop-valued with no DecidablePred. The same → Prop convention runs through the modal, temporal, and bimodal Kripke semantics.

I don't think there's a need to have two separate semantics.

You're already using attribute [local instance] Classical.propDecidable in StrongCompleteness.lean here.

Maybe just change canonicalValuation to

noncomputable def canonicalValuation (S : Set (PL.Proposition Atom)) : Valuation Atom :=
    fun p => decide (Proposition.atom p ∈ S)

...this does make the truth lemma more clumsy though; it would look like:

theorem prop_truth_lemma
    {S : Set (PL.Proposition Atom)}
    (h_mcs : PropSetMaximalConsistent PropositionalAxiom S) :
    (φ : PL.Proposition Atom) →
    (Evaluate (canonicalValuation S) φ = true ↔ φ ∈ S) := ...

On the other hand, I argue that this is still simpler and results in less code.

@ctchou also suggested that Bool.lean alone would suffice. The reason for Evaluate Prop-valued rather than collapsing everything through decide is uniformity with Kripke semantics since modal and temporal satisfaction (Satisfies) is inherently Prop-valued (accessibility relations, set membership at worlds), where the propositional Evaluate is the degenerate case — no worlds, no accessibility, same shape. If PL uses Bool but modal uses Prop, the FromPropositional embedding that lifts PL formulas into modal contexts has to bridge between the two evaluation types, which adds complexity rather than removing it.

One option would be to consolidate Bool.lean and Basic.lean into one file, keeping both evaluators with BoolEvaluate_eq_iff bridging them. The Modal/ and Temporal/ logics build on Evaluate (Prop-valued), while BoolEvaluate stays available for computable procedures like DPLL/SAT. I'm curious to get your thoughts on this.

It looks like @Thomas Waring has Prop based semantics in mind as well: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/pull/587/changes#diff-78912bb72e1c7000f8203f6312380447681f23b039101a86156ed6e3015836ccR35-R38

It also appears ωAcceptor is Prop based: https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/blob/70c5bf5874a1a511b32ad1ae605c07a13345d071/Cslib/Computability/Automata/Acceptors/OmegaAcceptor.lean#L17

Having all semantics be Prop based is awkward for decision procedures, where Evaluate model cnf where cnf : List (List (Literal Atom)) would naturally return Bool...

not exactly, that PR is still a draft, but the equivalent of the Bool semantics you suggest would be a HasInterp instance with Ground = Bool, the Prop part would just be saying that a proposition A is valid in that model if interp A = true — if we were to implement something like the classes i wrote in that PR i think we should absolutely have a way to define a computable evaluation function.

as i mentioned in a comment on cslib#648 and above i think the way to resolve the Prop / Bool issue is to define the interpretation for any docs#GeneralizedHeytingAlgebra, the typeclass inference would be able to specialise to either of those cases, and the soundness proof would go through for the general case. that way we also get Heyting algebra semantics for non-classical logics too.

Thomas Waring said:

that way we also get Heyting algebra semantics for non-classical logics too.

I think the zoo of non-classical logics may not always abide by Heyting algebra semantics; linear logics, for instance, don't always obey a ≤ b ⇨ c ↔ a ⊓ b ≤ c and instead have a separate residual for ⇨.

But now that I reread HasInterp, this looks like a good abstraction.
right, sure — i was referring to semantics specifically for PL in this case. there a generalized heyting algebra is exactly the structure you need to prove the soundness theorem.

Might be more appropriate to call it Cslib.Logic.Structural instead of Cslib.Logic.PL, but that's just being pedantic.

I do agree with @Ching-Tsun Chou about a separate bot constructor.

But with that in mind, I agree with @Thomas Waring that it would be nice if we could just have the following polymorphic Evaluate (although for HeytingAlgebras rather than GeneralizedHeytingAlgebras):

def Evaluate {Atom A : Type u} [HeytingAlgebra A]
    (v : Atom → A) : Proposition Atom → A
  | .atom p => v p
  | .bot => ⊥
  | .imp φ ψ => Evaluate v φ ⇨ Evaluate v ψ
  | .and φ ψ => Evaluate v φ ⊓ Evaluate v ψ
  | .or φ ψ => Evaluate v φ ⊔ Evaluate v ψ

with that definition of evaluate completeness is no longer true for minimal logic — this (i think) is why Benjamin's Kripke definitions need separate fields for the valuation of atoms and of bottom, which is avoided by just making ⊥ an atom itself.

for reference, this file has my development of algebraic semantics, including the evaluation function i propose — the general completeness theorem is:

theorem Theory.complete [Inhabited Atom] {A : Proposition Atom} :
    DerivableIn T A ↔
    ∀ {H : Type u} [GeneralizedHeytingAlgebra H] {v : Valuation Atom H}, (v ⊨ T) → v ⊨ A

where v ⊨ T (resp v ⊨ A) denotes that every axiom (resp the proposition A) is mapped to ⊤ under the valuation v. i find this very neat, but there is a tradeoff of course, you can remove the v ⊨ T hypothesis for T = IPL (resp CPL) by requiring that H is a HeytingAlgebra (resp BooleanAlgebra) and that v ⊥ = ⊥. (Note that in Benjamin's development a similar thing happens, where ISemanticConsequence specialises IForces by requiring that ⊥ is never forced.)

Thomas Waring said:

Hmm, I've never seen anything like @Benjamin Brast-McKie's botForces for Kripke semantics for intuitionistic logic before... I wonder why it's needed.

Anyway, you can strengthen your completeness theorem to HeytingAlgebras using Dedekind-MacNeille completion. Here is a modification to your branch where this is proved. Normally, this would establish that IPL is a conservative extension of MPL, although I'm not sure we can prove it given how we are handling ⊥.

oh very nice! thanks for that — i'd actually been looking for a semantic way to show that IPL is conservative over MPL, and that was one of the reasons i wanted to allow substitutions which don't preserve ⊥.

unfortunately it doesn't address my concern, because that result requires allowing valuations v where v ⊥ ≠ ⊥, so the problem is with the definition of evaluate, not the restriction to Heyting algebras. that's also why Benjamin's definitions require a separate field specifying the valuation of ⊥, because if it was always mapped to false / a bottom element then every model would validate efq.

Thomas Waring said:

unfortunately it doesn't address my concern, because that result requires allowing valuations v where v ⊥ ≠ ⊥, so the problem is with the definition of evaluate, not the restriction to Heyting algebras. that's also why Benjamin's definitions require a separate field specifying the valuation of ⊥, because if it was always mapped to false / a bottom element then every model would validate efq.

Well, I'm still a proponent of an explicit falsum in the base syntax (and thus EFQ). It's more natural to have separate syntax for positive fragments IMO. Aside from minimal logic, there's also IPL〈∧, →, ⊤〉 for CCCs and IPL〈→, ⊤〉, which is the essential logic for the deduction theorem and corresponds to typed SKI combinators via Curry-Howard.

For the purposes of DPLL, having ⊥ : Atom adds some extra complexity, since pos ⊥ has to be removed from every clause and clauses with neg ⊥ need to be removed. Also, additional care is needed to ensure v ⊥ = ⊥ for any valuation v the algorithm outputs.

Thomas is right that MPL completeness requires valuations where ⊥ is not mapped to the algebra's bottom — that's exactly what bot_val (and botForces on the Kripke side) are for. The question is whether this freedom should come from making ⊥ an atom or from an explicit parameter on the evaluator.

The strongest reason to keep ⊥ as a primitive constructor is substitution invariance. Formulas over Atom form the free algebra over the signature {⊥, →, ∧, ∨}. Substitution σ : Atom → Proposition Atom' is the unique homomorphism extending σ — monadic bind. With primitive ⊥, we get | .bot => .bot in the substitution function: ⊥ is a nullary operation in the signature, fixed by every substitution. Axiom schemes like ⊥ → A are automatically closed under substitution — applying σ gives ⊥ → σ(A), not σ(⊥) → σ(A).

With ⊥ as an atom, bind σ sends ⊥ ↦ σ(⊥), which can be anything. Every theorem about substitution closure (we currently have subst_preserves_axiom, subst_preserves_intAxiom, subst_preserves_minAxiom, hilbertSubstitution, Theory.Derivation.substAtom) acquires a side condition σ(⊥) = ⊥. The intended substitutions no longer correspond to the full Kleisli category — you're working in a subcategory of ⊥-preserving maps where the universal property fails.

The same point manifests in universal algebra. ⊥ is a nullary operation symbol — same ontological kind as → and ∧. Atoms are generators; connectives (including nullary ones) are operations that determine what "homomorphism" means in the signature. ⊥ along with the other connectives are the logical constants with fixed semantic clauses; atoms provide the non-logical vocabulary subject to interpretation. That ⊥ deserves to be among the logical constants follows from the inadequacy of the v ⊥ = ⊥ constraint, which is external to the definition of satisfaction: it must be stated as a hypothesis, verified when constructing models, and preserved under model-theoretic operations (submodels, products, ultraproducts, canonical models).

These matters are obscured but still present in minimal logic, which has no axioms constraining the interpretation of ⊥. But "arbitrary nullary operator" and "arbitrary atom" are not the same: an operator is fixed under substitution; an atom is not. Even though ⊥ has no axioms constraining its denotation, its interpretation in a given algebra is a free parameter — it needs to map to something. The bot_val parameter provides exactly this: ⊥ evaluates to a fixed-but-unconstrained element of the algebra, the same element throughout the evaluation. With ⊥-as-atom, substitution can replace ⊥ with a different formula entirely, which is a different degree of freedom than varying its interpretation.

Re cost comparison — bot_val adds one argument to AlgEvaluate and one field (botForces) to the Kripke semantics. With ⊥-as-atom, every substitution theorem gets a side condition, every algorithm that builds valuations needs to ensure v ⊥ = ⊥, and [Bot Atom] propagates through every theorem statement. Matthew's DPLL point illustrates the pattern: the constraint v ⊥ = ⊥ is doing the work of a semantic clause that should be part of the definition of satisfaction.

Thomas's completeness theorem is genuinely elegant with the v ⊨ t framing — and it works just as well with primitive ⊥ and bot_val: the general theorem quantifies over (v, bot_val), the v ⊨ t hypothesis does all the work, and specializing to ipl forces bot_val = ⊥ via the efq axioms (since bot_val ⇨ x = ⊤ for all x implies bot_val ≤ x for all x). so the parametric completeness architecture is orthogonal to the proposition type design — we can and should adopt the v ⊨ t style regardless.

Anyhow, this is what I have come to so far, but curious to get your thoughts.

Hi both, sorry I haven't gotten back to this earlier. I think perhaps the essential disagreement comes from something I maybe could have communicated better — what I've formalised is minimal natural deduction, the definitions of IPL and CPL should probably be seen as encodings, rather than a once-and-for-all definition. My definitions make sense in this setting because I want to allow ⊥ to be absent, so having it as a primitive constructor makes no sense. I picked MPL (rather than IPL or any of the other interesting fragments Matthew mentioned) because it is expressive enough to encode the others (using the ⊥ : Atom construction) while still being minimal in terms of number of rules / constructors. The issue at hand is I think whether we want MPL encoded as a fragment of IPL, or IPL encoded in MPL via the theory construction.

If we were to add ⊥ to the proposition type, I think we should also add efq to the derivation type — a big part of the appeal of natural deduction is the symmetry introduction / elimination and the close match between formula constructors and inference rules. From the free-algebra perspective, minimal logic doesn't want ⊥ as a constructor — a docs#GeneralizedHeytingAlgebra is not an algebra over the signature with ⊥, which is why you need the extra unnatural field botVal. If we add the constructor to the signature, we should also interpret it, which adds the rule efq to the derivation type, and makes the interpretation land in docs#HeytingAlgebra.

I've laid out a potential comprise in this branch, defining intuitionistic propositions and derivations, and the translations with our existing framework. As Matthew mentioned, we will want to talk about various fragments at some point, but how exactly to do that most ergonomically is an ongoing discussion. (btw Benjamin, why did you delete that part of the docstring in NaturalDeduction/Basic?) While it's certainly possible to define MPL as a fragment of IPL, whether or not that is actually better than defining a separate inductive type for each remains to be seen. The development I linked here should be seen as a proof-of-concept, but it shows that it is relatively straightforward to translate from one system to another. This frees up developments such as Matthew's DPLL to use a proposition type appropriate to their application, eg Benjamin your Łukasiewicz convention would make sense for a classical proposition type.

I'm still not exactly convinced re the cost issue, unfortunately. If you have, eg, the bot_val field in your definition of valuation, then you still need to ensure for intuitionistic applications that v ⊥ = ⊥. You made a separate definition for IForces if i remember correctly, which could be encoded simply as a subtype.

Anyway, if the community strongly wants IPL as the base theory, we should of course do that — this message is my reasoning for the version I picked when I wrote these files. In other parts of CSLib, we have accepted that we might need different conventions / definitions for different applications — I care about proofs and computation interpretations of logic, not provability, so it make sense to consider natural deduction (rather than a more metalogically convenient system) and a weak fragment — but other applications might have different needs (like DPLL for example). Too many definitions could be a source of tech debt, but i don't think it's something we should write off altogether.

Thanks for the thoughtful discussion, Thomas and Matthew. I've worked through Thomas's intuitionistic branch and investigated whether a typeclass-based split could avoid the hybrid ND design. Here are my conclusions so far.

On ⊥ as a primitive constructor

I remain convinced that primitive ⊥ provides the best approach, and I think the thread has substantially converged on this. From my perspective, the decisive argument is substitution invariance. ⊥ is a nullary connective rather than a propositional variable. With ⊥-as-atom, every substitution theorem acquires a σ(⊥) = ⊥ side condition. With ⊥-as-constructor, this is automatic: the monad bind case | .bot => .bot requires no condition. CSLib's substitution results — subst_preserves_axiom, subst_preserves_intAxiom, hilbertSubstitution, Theory.Derivation.substAtom — all work cleanly because of this. The FromPropositional embeddings to Modal and Temporal logic also benefit: the map | .bot => .bot is direct, with no special-case handling.

The ND symmetry trade-off

Thomas, your ND symmetry point makes sense. Natural deduction's appeal — as Gentzen articulated it — is that each connective's meaning is given by its introduction and elimination rules. With ⊥ in the syntax, pure ND symmetry would demand that its elimination rule (efq) be a primitive constructor of Derivation. CSLib's current design breaks this: ⊥ has a syntax constructor but no derivation constructor.

The cost of preserving ND symmetry (your IProposition/IDerivation design) is that it duplicates the entire formula API — monad instance, substitution lemmas, DecidableEq, three evaluation functions, two bridge lemmas, and the two FromPropositional embeddings. For a library building upward through Modal, Temporal, and Bimodal logics that all share Proposition, that is a permanent maintenance multiplier.

There is also a logical reason to accept the hybrid. ⊥ is the one connective with no introduction rule in any proof system. Every other connective has both intro and elim rules; ⊥ has only elimination. The asymmetry is a property of ⊥ itself, not of our design. Making efq a theory axiom rather than a derivation constructor reflects this directly: it is absent in MPL (where ⊥ has no special proof-theoretic status) and present in IPL/CPL as a logic-dependent rule.

I've updated the ## Implementation notes section of NaturalDeduction/Basic.lean to state this trade-off factually — naming both sides and linking to this thread — rather than presenting the design as settled. I've also restored your original references (Prawitz, Troelstra & Van Dalen, Sorensen & Urzyczyn), which were inadvertently dropped during the ND overhaul.

btw Benjamin, why did you delete that part of the docstring in NaturalDeduction/Basic?

The deletion was a mistake during the ND overhaul (commit 80f54485, task 173) which removed the botE constructor and added six rules and treated the docstring as a clean-slate rewrite. The ## Implementation notes section has been restored with your original framing (plus an expanded explanation of the trade-off). All four of your original references are back, along with a link to this thread.

On bot_val: Johansson's designated constant

The bot_val : H parameter in AlgEvaluate is not a patch — it is the designated constant of Johansson algebras. In Johansson's original minimal logic (1937), models are algebraic structures that may or may not have a bottom element, and when they do, its interpretation is a free parameter. bot_val captures exactly this degree of freedom. For IPL, fixing bot_val = ⊥ recovers the standard Heyting algebra semantics. For MPL, quantifying over all bot_val values is what makes MPL completeness true: if bot_val were forced to ⊥, every model would validate efq, collapsing MPL into IPL. This parallels botForces in KripkeModel.

On the parametric completeness style

Thomas's v ⊨ T framing is elegant and general, and I completely agree it should be the canonical statement. It is already adopted: AlgTValid in Semantics/Algebra.lean implements exactly this pattern, and the general completeness theorem Theory.alg_complete uses it. The tier-specific corollaries (MPL.alg_complete, IPL.alg_complete, alg_complete_classical) specialize the algebra type and bot_val, giving the clean statements you described. I've also added docstrings to all definitions in Semantics/Algebra/Completeness.lean explaining the Lindenbaum construction, which was previously undocumented.

On Prop vs. Bool semantics

The dual-evaluator approach resolves this. Evaluate (Prop-valued) is needed for canonical model construction: MCS membership fun p => atom p ∈ S is irreducibly Prop-valued and non-computable. BoolEvaluate (Bool-valued) is there for DPLL and SAT. The bridge lemmas propEvaluateEq and boolEvaluateEq in Semantics/Algebra/Bridge.lean connect both to AlgEvaluate, confirming they are special cases of the algebraic framework. Matthew, your DPLL work can build entirely on the BoolEvaluate layer without touching the metatheory.

On the typeclass split question

I investigated three approaches to avoid the hybrid ND using typeclasses. None can eliminate it without duplicating the formula type. Lean 4's inductive type system does not support conditionally-available constructors: you cannot make efq a constructor of Derivation only when a typeclass is satisfied. Options B (split at Derivation level) and C (typeclass on connectives) both collapse back to either the current design or Thomas's Option A (separate IDerivation). I also share Matthew's concern about conservative extension proofs: with separate formula types, IPL is conservative over MPL becomes a theorem about a translation function rather than a subset relation on derivations, which is harder to state cleanly.

Thomas, your IProposition/IDerivation branch demonstrates that the translation is mechanically possible — propEquiv, toDerivation, and toIDerivation all compile, and the translations are proved correct. This is valuable as a reference. But the noncomputable toIDerivation direction (which uses Classical.choose) means you cannot compute with intuitionistic derivations built by translation, and the maintenance cost of the duplication table above is substantial.
